Locks
LOKS
n. pl.
From Anglo-Saxon locc, a tress of hair. Webster 1828: a tuft or ringlet of hair. In the Nazarite law the uncut locks are the visible sign of a vow, and in Samson they became the most famous hair in Scripture.

Biblical Definition

The Nazarite vow had three marks — no wine, no contact with the dead, and no razor — and only the third could be seen: All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head... he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow (Numbers 6:5). The hair is not the strength; it is the sign of the separation, which is why its loss mattered. Delilah works toward that sign by degrees: If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web (Judges 16:13), and Samson, playing with the secret, gives away its neighbourhood before he gives away the thing. Ezekiel legislates the priestly mean between two extremes: Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads (Ezekiel 44:20) — neither the mourner’s shaven head nor the Nazarite’s long growth, but a trimmed and unremarkable ordinariness. And the Song uses the word for a lover kept waiting in the night: my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night (Song of Solomon 5:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LOCK, in this sense, as a tuft or ringlet of hair; a tress; and in the plural, the hair of the head collectively.

expand to see more

LOCK, n. — A tuft of hair; a ringlet or tress.

In the plural, the hair of the head; as, hoary locks.

A tuft of wool or other fibrous substance.

Distinct from LOCK, an instrument to fasten a door, though the two words are spelled alike.

Anglo-Saxon locc, a lock of hair; compare German Locke.

Key Scripture

Numbers 6:5 — "All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow."

Judges 16:13 — "And Delilah said unto Samson, Hitherto thou hast mocked me, and told me lies: tell me wherewith thou mightest be bound. And he said unto her, If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web."

Ezekiel 44:20 — "Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads."

Song of Solomon 5:2 — "I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night."

Modern Corruption

Samson’s hair is popularly treated as a magic charm, which misses the point of the narrative: the hair was a sign of consecration, and what he lost was the LORD.

expand to see more

The retelling that makes Samson’s strength reside in his hair turns a covenant narrative into a folk tale, and Judges is careful to prevent it. When the locks are cut the text does not say his strength departed but something far graver: he wist not that the LORD was departed from him (Judges 16:20). The strength was never in the hair; the hair was the visible token of a separation to God, and the LORD who gave the strength withdrew when the vow was finally discarded. Note also the manner of the loss — not a single betrayal but a sequence of games with the secret, each one closer, until the thing itself was surrendered to a lap. That is how consecration is usually lost, and it is why the sign mattered: a visible mark makes a private erosion harder to hide.

Ezekiel 44:20 is worth setting alongside, because it legislates against both extremes and the balance is instructive. Priests were forbidden the shaven head (the mourner’s and the pagan’s sign) and forbidden long-grown locks (the Nazarite’s sign); they were to poll their heads — trimmed, ordinary, unremarkable. God’s ministers were not to be identifiable by a striking appearance in either direction. There is a standing application in that for those who serve the church, and it cuts against the instinct to mark out spiritual seriousness by conspicuous difference. The Reformers made a related point against clerical costume and tonsure: the minister is a man among men, distinguished by office and doctrine rather than by hair.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pera (H6545), long hair, the loose locks of a Nazarite; machlaphah (H4253), a braid or plait; nazir (H5139), one separated, a Nazarite.

expand to see more

Hebrew pera (H6545) — the loose or long hair of the head; the locks of the hair of his head (Numbers 6:5) and the forbidden growth of Ezekiel 44:20.

Hebrew machlaphah (H4253) — a braid or plait; the seven locks of my head (Judges 16:13).

Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated or consecrated; the Nazarite whose uncut hair is the sign.

Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor; the instrument forbidden all the days of the vow.

Hebrew kasam (H3697) — to shear or poll; the priestly trimming commanded in Ezekiel 44:20.

Usage

"He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow (Numbers 6:5) — the one mark of the vow that could be seen."

"If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web (Judges 16:13) — the secret given away by degrees."

"Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long (Ezekiel 44:20) — the priestly mean between two conspicuous extremes."
